items.excerpt:
Known for playing with County Joe McDonald, and for her experimental sound band The United States of America, Dorothy Moskowitz came back in 2023 with United States of Alchemy and their well-received release,
Under an Endless Sky
.
In collaboration with avant-garde composer and filmmaker Francesco Paolo Paladino, and poet and music writer Luca Chino Ferrari,
Songs of Compassion
is eleven songs containing subversive and at times beautiful music, and richly evocative lyrics.
Francesco Paolo Paladi
items.body: Known for playing with County Joe McDonald, and for her experimental sound band The United States of America, Dorothy Moskowitz came back in 2023 with United States of Alchemy and their well-received release, Under an Endless Sky . In collaboration with avant-garde composer and filmmaker Francesco Paolo Paladino, and poet and music writer Luca Chino Ferrari, Songs of Compassion is eleven songs containing subversive and at times beautiful music, and richly evocative lyrics. Francesco Paolo Paladino and Luca Chino Ferrari | Photo by Maria Assunta Karini Songs of Compassion has two challenges for the listener. The first is the music, called variously avant-garde, ambient, modal, non-linear, and a few more. It is played mostly on pianos mixed in and out of the foreground, sometimes doubled, and sometimes out of phase, joined by strings, woodwinds, synth washes, and steely sounds. Initially disorienting, the music serves to remind us how locked our minds are to Western notions of harmonic movement. It speaks of alternative musical narratives much older and much further away. They are songs that subvert the song: more like Steve Reich than Steve Stills; more like Phillip Glass than Phil Collins. UNITED STATES OF ALCHEMY - Pale Wanderer At the same time, there are the poetic yet strikingly contemporary lyrics. �Pale Wanderer� talks about the fact that authoritarianism needs willing accomplices, describing what happens �When you make a deal with darkness.� UNITED STATES OF ALCHEMY (Dorothy Moskowitz, Francesco Paolo Paladino e Luka Chino Ferrari) by Silentes �Charlottesville� (written with the late Joe Byrd) evokes the time not long ago when torch-wielding nazis, proud of the metaphoric Ns on their tunics, chanted the antisemitic tropes paraphrased in Moskowitz�s words, �We�ll be one people, pure of race/No greedy throng could take our place� . Besides the overtly political lyrics, in the tradition of 1960s protest songs, there are also thoughtful meditations on mortality and our place in the universe. The message is high-minded yet sincere and direct. World weary and wise, Moskowitz�s voice inhabits the evocative philosophical lyrics with the authority of a skilled method actor. The melodies unfold like streams of consciousness, rising and falling, not following expected diatonic chord progressions, but honouring, instead, the value of each word. Moskowitz�s piano acts as another voice and sometimes a kind of Greek chorus commenting on the proceedings. The surrounding music frames, creates pulses and dissonances, and shimmers. The return of Dorothy Moskowitz with her renamed project has arrived in a moment quite similar to the times that spawned its predecessor. Political division, unrest, and uncertainty always generate artistic reaction, and United States of Alchemy roared back to life with their epic 24-minute opening track �Under an Endless Sky� in 2023, serving perhaps as an �In-A-Gadda-Da-Vida� for our times. Songs of Compassion continues to challenge how we think about our world. It�s music that defies the song form, while doing exactly what music is supposed to do�enrich the human condition. Find the artist online. The title track from the 2023 U.S. of Alchemy recording Under an Endless Sky by Dorothy Moskowitz & United States of Alchemy Further reading Cris Derksen - The Visit (Review) Tiny Sun - Vanishment (Review) Maria Ka - Di Mashin (Review) Further listening You will find a number of Dorothy Moskowitz's works on Race The Sky , most recently on Podgrammes #022 and #019.
items.label: Songs of Compassion
items._cn_summary: Dorothy Moskowitz与意大利作曲家Paladino、作家Ferrari组成的United States of Alchemy项目，延续了她在1960年代The United States of America乐队时期的实验精神。《Songs of Compassion》以十一首曲目构建了一套反叛西方传统和声逻辑的聆听框架，钢琴在前景与背景之间游移，与弦乐、木管、合成器织体和金属质感声响相互缠绕。乐评将其比作Steve Reich与Philip Glass的极简主义路径，而非流行旋律的展开方式。歌词层面同样具有明确的政治锋芒，从Charlottesville事件中的纳粹意象到对威权主义共谋的剖析，沿袭六十年代抗议歌曲脉络的同时也触及对死亡与宇宙位置的哲学冥思。Moskowitz的演唱承载着岁月沉淀的权威感，旋律如意识流般起伏，不遵循功能和声，而是让每个词语获得自身的分量。

items.body: Sendas by Omar Sosa True to a Monk-inspired commitment never to play the same thing twice, Cuban pianist and composer Omar Sosa�s Sendas (Pathways), his latest solo offering, is the vivid invention of a pensive, restlessly creative, evolutionary artistry. As with all Sosa�s work, Sendas is the fortunate product of serendipity. In 2021 the COVID lockdown was underway, his marriage was ending, and a scheduled Milan appearance cancellation garnered an invitation to record at the Fazioli Pianoforti Concert Hall, annex to the renowned Italian piano manufactory in Sacile, Pordenone, about an hour northeast of Venice. At Fazioli, Sosa found himself in august company. Herbie Hancock and a host of classical pianists are Fazioli artists. Among the institutions that have embraced the Fazioli sound are the Juilliard School, Teatro La Fenice (Venice), the Budapest Palace of Arts, the Paris Conservatory, the Beijing Grand Theatre, and the universities of Salzburg, Graz, and Vienna. An unscripted two-hour solo improvisation on a Fazioli grand in the empty concert hall provided the raw audio for Sendas , later to be flavored in the mix, sparsely, with voice clips, percussion, loops, field recordings, found sounds effects that Sosa has collected over a career spanning four decades. As Sosa related to me soon after completing the post-production of Sendas , �Humanity is spiritually lost. We humans are all in this together. We need to evolve, but always keeping the traditions, walking with a strong, determined pace. We need more grounded music with overtones that resonate with the lower chakras� like throat singing, a mantra of the universal music.� �Creativity is about combining all your influences in a new way. I don�t aspire to be jazz, Latin, timba, reggaeton, classical. I avoid styles, but I respect the forms.� �I try not to think about how listeners will receive it but I do try to address their expectations, and go with the music to some other new place. Many free spirits come to listen, to be a part of the journey we are on.� Sosa laughs, �My son says, �Your niche is really small.� But the people who come really are there to be part of what we are going to do.� �Economics, technology, the streaming ear wash, algorithms all want to put you into a defined category � and so do many music journalists! The industry�s mentality is that any investment in artists must be defined by market categories to be profitable.� �But I play to be free of that,� Sosa says. �I play without thinking. There are no wrong notes. I love the first take. That�s the take, the natural voice of your soul. �Less is more� is a mantra in my life and music.� Consider the opening of �Inside the Spirit,� easing in leisurely, reaching over the keyboard into the resonant heart of the instrument, plucking and stroking the strings, teasing out a fuller resonance � only later to be embellished in the studio mix with light percussion and the muted Spanish-language refrain of a pregonero or street vendor, as might be heard in the calles of Havana or any other Latin American barrio. Sendas by Omar Sosa Moving from the secular to the sacred, �Deities Serenade� is an Afro-Cuban invocation of the shape-shifting divine, yet with ample room for ecumenical recasting in accord with a listener�s own self-location. �Inside My Soul� and �Something from Home� are Sosa works that to my ear may be an intuitive response to the distant call of Chopin�s "Nocturnes," to which Sosa says he listened every night for two years as a conservatory student in Cuba. Sendas by Omar Sosa �Caribbean Movement� and �Shirma� speak to Sosa�s rootedness in the lyrical, rhythmic, and harmonic heritage of the plantation islands where African and European cultures tragically entwined. In the violent forging of the world�s first truly modern people, social, cultural, linguistic, and musical displacements proved more flexible and accommodating than many of those same people, who shaped a contentious convergence of traditions into a changing same that persists into the unfolding present, ever yet to come. With expressive transcendence such as this, seeking to reduce the spiritual essence and inspiration of Sosa�s music to words is rather a fool�s errand. Better rather to listen, to contemplate, to perceive the pathway, to wander the sonic sendas coursing to the next way station without prejudice or preconception. To that end, Scott Price, Sosa�s longtime manager and friend relates, �We are using Sendas as the springboard for our first experiments in AI-generated Omar Sosa music videos.� Absent the opportunity to see and hear Sosa perform live, the palpable ideal, these ancillary audiovisual experiments further the ineffability of his artistic quest, the unique nature of the listening experience and all that ensues.

The track is the third single from Ignea’s upcoming album “Monumental,” due October 23, 2026 via Napalm Records, and pairs Ignea vocalist Helle Bohdanova with LaPlegua on an industrial metal cut built around aggrotech and electro-industrial textures. “Prefab” looks at architecture and collective memory, themes that run through “Monumental,” which
items.body: Ukrainian modern metal band Ignea have released a new single, Prefab, featuring Andy LaPlegua of Combichrist. The track is the third single from Ignea’s upcoming album “Monumental,” due October 23, 2026 via Napalm Records, and pairs Ignea vocalist Helle Bohdanova with LaPlegua on an industrial metal cut built around aggrotech and electro-industrial textures. “Prefab” looks at architecture and collective memory, themes that run through “Monumental,” which the band describes as centered on nostalgia. Bohdanova wrote the lyrics; the music was composed by keyboardist Yevhenii Zhytniuk with additional contributions from Bohdanova. Bohdanova commented on the track: “‘Prefab’ reflects on the darker side of nostalgia – prefabricated socialist buildings, originally meant to give everyone a roof over their heads. But like many socialist ideals, the concept was flawed at its core: uniform, industrial, stripping people of individuality and personal choice, making them feel like ants inside their own homes. Remnants of this architecture still stand across Europe – from Ukraine and Poland, from Germany to France. As Ukrainians from a post-Soviet country, we grew up surrounded by the physical remains of a system that promised a bright future and delivered the opposite. In the ‘Prefab’ video, we wanted to convey the feeling of a confined, uniform space, a cramped room representing a typical Soviet apartment, where only the tenants ever change. When we shaped the demo, we were basically hearing Andy’s vocals in the back of our minds, and we’re so glad he agreed to lend his voice. Having Combichrist as part of the industrial metal track on our upcoming album […]” Andy LaPlegua formed Combichrist in 2003 as a solo studio project, building it into one of the touchstone acts of the aggrotech and industrial metal scenes alongside his other projects Icon of Coil and Panzer AG. Combichrist’s most recent album, “The Venom In The Mouth Of God,” was announced via Out Of Line Music earlier in 2026, following singles including “Demons Wanna Be Summoned” with King 810 and “Feraline.” “Monumental” is Ignea’s second full-length album, following 2023’s “Dreams of Lands Unseen.” Writing and recording took place largely during the winter of 2025-2026, amid icy temperatures and long power outages in Kyiv during the full-scale war in Ukraine. Bohdanova described the record’s concept: “Back in the 17th century, nostalgia was considered a deadly disease – and in many ways, it still is. Much of this album was inspired by modernist architecture – concrete giants built to signal progress and a brighter future, now slowly decaying.” The album spans nine tracks: “Darkness,” “Dreams of Lands Unseen,” “Presence of the Past,” “Prefab” (feat. Combichrist), “What Buildings Dream of,” “I am in Hell,” “Between No Longer and Not Yet,” “Harmony Manufactured” (feat. Hiraes), and “Nadir.” Mixing and mastering were handled by Grammy-nominated producer Jacob Hansen, whose credits include Delain, Amaranthe, Volbeat, Amon Amarth, Arch Enemy and Epica. “Monumental” arrives on translucent dark night blue splatter vinyl with booklet, solid silver vinyl, CD jewelcase, a CD/T-shirt bundle, and digitally, released via Napalm Records. Ignea will support Evergrey’s “Architects Of A New Weave” European tour alongside Stellar Circuits starting in November, taking “Prefab” and the rest of “Monumental” to stages across Scandinavia, the UK and mainland Europe. Ignea tour dates 11 November 2026 – Lund, Sweden – Mejeriet 12 November 2026 – Stockholm, Sweden – Kollektivet Livet 13 November 2026 – Linkoping, Sweden – Paletset 14 November 2026 – Gothenburg, Sweden – Filmstudion 2 15 November 2026 – Oslo, Norway – Salt 17 November 2026 – Hamburg, Germany – Logo 18 November 2026 – Berlin, Germany – Hole44 19 November 2026 – Munich, Germany – Feierwerk 20 November 2026 – Vienna, Austria – Weberknecht 21 November 2026 – Milan, Italy – Slaughter Club 22 November 2026 – Aarau, Switzerland – KiFF 23 November 2026 – Antwerp, Belgium – Zappa 25 November 2026 – Southampton, UK – The Brook 26 November 2026 – Birmingham, UK – Asylum 27 November 2026 – London, UK – The Underworld 28 November 2026 – Leeds, UK – The Key Club 29 November 2026 – Dublin, Ireland – Opium 30 November 2026 – Belfast, UK – Limelight 2 1 December 2026 – Glasgow, UK – G2 2 December 2026 – Newcastle, UK – Anarchy Brew 3 December 2026 – Manchester, UK – Rebellion 4 December 2026 – Bristol, UK – Strange Brew 5 December 2026 – Nottingham, UK – Saltbox 7 December 2026 – Paris, France – Petit Bain 8 December 2026 – Trier, Germany – Mergener Hof 9 December 2026 – Karlsruhe, Germany – Substage 10 December 2026 – Dortmund, Germany – Junkyard 11 December 2026 – Rotterdam, Netherlands – Baroeg 12 December 2026 – Maastricht, Netherlands – Muziekgieterij About Ignea Ignea formed in Ukraine in 2013, releasing the EP “Sputnik” the same year. The band mixes melodic and progressive metal with symphonic, electronic and folk elements, building material around narrative concepts. Ignea’s debut full-length, “The Sign of Faith,” followed in 2017. The band’s early single “Alga,” released as a hymn referencing the Crimean Tatars’ battle cry after the annexation of Crimea, became the first original song by a Ukrainian metal band recorded with a full symphonic orchestra. Ignea’s second album, “The Realms of Fire and Death” (2020), was funded through the band’s Patreon page and was later named Ukraine’s metal album of the year. A split EP with Ersedu, “BESTIA,” followed in 2021. After building an independent following through two albums and two EPs, Ignea signed to Napalm Records and released “Dreams of Lands Unseen” in 2023, an album dedicated to Ukrainian travel writer and photographer Sofia Yablonska. Despite the ongoing war, the band toured extensively, including a 43-date EU/UK run supporting Fear Factory, and has since played festivals including Wacken Open Air, Summer Breeze, Bloodstock and Brutal Assault, alongside club dates with Cradle of Filth, Epica and Butcher Babies. Nine Ignea tracks also feature in the video game “S.T.A.L.K.E.R. 2: Heart of Chornobyl.” The current lineup is Helle Bohdanova (vocals), Yevhenii Zhytniuk (keyboards), Dmytro Vinnichenko (guitars) and Oleksandr Kamyshyn (bass). Ignea’s second full-length, “Monumental,” follows “Dreams of Lands Unseen” on October 23, 2026, led by the singles “Prefab” featuring Andy LaPlegua and its predecessors, and supported by the band’s November-December European tour with Evergrey.

items._cn_summary: 乌克兰现代金属乐队Ignea发布新单曲《Prefab》，与Combichrist主脑Andy LaPlegua合作，以工业金属为骨架融合aggrotech与electro-industrial的电子质感。歌曲主题围绕预制板式社会主义建筑展开，探讨集体记忆与怀旧——从东欧到西欧，这类被承诺美好未来的建筑如今成为冰冷的遗迹。歌词由主唱Helle Bohdanova撰写，键盘手Yevhenii Zhytniuk主导作曲，战争背景下在严寒与停电的基辅完成录制。整张专辑《Monumental》以九首作品延续对现代主义建筑、记忆与衰败的反思，将金属的重量感与工业电子的机械脉冲结合，乌克兰后苏联视角为作品增添了独特的地域文化厚度。

items.body: Laho is a Finnish project that originated in 2006. After releasing a few records during its early years, the project went quiet for a long time before being reactivated a few years ago. “Death Machines”—which feels more like a seven-track mini-album—was inspired by today’s dystopian world, as well as by self-reflection and other dark themes. The music is indeed quite dark, but that is not the whole story. This record reveals two sides: on the one hand, a powerful production featuring menacing yet brilliant basslines topped with razor-sharp sequences; on the other, a completely different style with a Cinematic feel, including one entirely instrumental track. Personally, I prefer Laho’s harder side, which occasionally reminds me of early Combichrist, albeit with a certain polished touch. This is also evident in the vocal production, which is powerful yet has something of a ‘Power-Pop’ quality. It comes as no surprise, then, that the album concludes with a remarkable cover of Depeche Mode‘s “Behind the Wheel,” delivered in a dark and intense style. I think it’s a great track, by the way. Laho seems to be a sort of Janus—a two-faced project, with its powerful side completely winning me over. (Rating:7½). Listen to “The Great Collapse”: The Great Collapse by Laho About Laho Laho is a Finnish dark electronic project led by musician and recording engineer Konsta Vehkala, who is based in Jyväskylä and is responsible for all composition, programming and production. The project is an outlet for solo works by Vehkala and blends industrial, EBM, futurepop and darkwave. The project began in 2006 under the name Lahonnut Konkelo as a series of electronic and industrial experiments. The name was shortened to Laho shortly afterwards. The first EP, “The Other Side”, appeared in 2007 as an independently issued CDr, combining instrumental industrial metal with a slightly experimental edge. It was later re-released by Italian netlabel Ekleipsi, which also issued the first full-length album “Escape from the Dying Star” in 2009. “Escape from the Dying Star” was recorded between 2007 and 2008 at the Cable_Hell studio and released digitally in April 2009, offering a mix of electro-industrial, cybernetic synth work and distorted guitar. The album held ten tracks including “Program”, “Dead End” and a remix by Technomancer. Later in 2009 Laho issued “The World in Flames” as a standalone digital release, followed by the single “Mechanigod” in 2011 and a one-off digital track “Walking in the Air (1984 mix)” in December 2021. After these early EP and album releases, the project entered a 13-year hiatus as Vehkala focused on other bands and production work. Writing for Laho resumed in 2024, leading to a new series of songs, this time including vocals. Parallel to Laho, Vehkala maintains an active role in the Finnish metal scene. He plays drums for the melodic metal band Psychework and has performed and recorded with groups including Gian, Vipermilk and Lojohh, as well as contributing recording, mixing and mastering work to a wide range of Finnish underground acts. “Death Machines” is Laho’s first release since writing resumed in 2024, and its first EP built around vocals throughout.
items._genre: darkwave / industrial / EBM / futurepop / dark electronic
items._cn_summary: 芬兰暗潮工业项目Laho沉寂十三年后回归，带来这张融合EBM与未来流行的数字EP。整体风格呈现两面性：一面以低频贝斯线与锐利序列构成高强度工业节拍，辅以力量感的人声处理；另一面引入电影化氛围，包含一首纯器乐曲目。创作受当下反乌托邦现实与自我反思启发，歌词与编制均倾向于冷峻、机械化的情绪表达。专辑以重新演绎Depeche Mode经典《Behind the Wheel》作结，将原作转化为更具压迫感的暗色版本。制作上由Konsta Vehkala独立完成，录音与混音均体现出一定的技术功底，但整体仍属于类型框架内的扎实作品，实验性与突破性有限。适合暗潮与工业电子场景下的循环聆听。

items.album: Shadowlands festival adds 16 more acts for its Canterbury debut in July 2027
items.excerpt: Shadowlands, a new international music festival at the Gulbenkian Arts Centre in Canterbury, England, has added 16 acts to its debut edition running 1-4 July 2027, bringing the final line-up to 35 names across the alternative, electronic, avant-garde and experimental fields. The additions, announced 10 September, include These New Puritans, Matmos, Årabrot, Hula, Barry Adamson, Sunroof, JG Thirlwell (solo), Negativland, Globo, The Soft Pink Truth, Carl Stone, 2nd Gen, Mischievous Misappropriator
items.body: Shadowlands, a new international music festival at the Gulbenkian Arts Centre in Canterbury, England, has added 16 acts to its debut edition running 1-4 July 2027, bringing the final line-up to 35 names across the alternative, electronic, avant-garde and experimental fields. The additions, announced 10 September, include These New Puritans, Matmos, Årabrot, Hula, Barry Adamson, Sunroof, JG Thirlwell (solo), Negativland, Globo, The Soft Pink Truth, Carl Stone, 2nd Gen, Mischievous Misappropriators, Monosum, M.C. Schmidt and Obel Feldi, and Rangelova as DJ. The festival launched on 2 July with 19 acts already confirmed, among them Foetus performing as a 20-piece chamber orchestra, Lustmord, Test Dept., Clock DVA, The Wolfgang Press, Portion Control, :Zoviet*France, Warrington-Runcorn New Town Development Plan, Regis (with Liam Andrews) and People Like Us. The event spans three performance spaces on the University of Kent campus, alongside a programme of talks, Q&As and film screenings. Several of the new additions mark returns or firsts. Sheffield industrial funk band Hula are reforming for their first live show in almost four decades. Barry Adamson is premiering a new solo show, “Gone Undercover.” JG Thirlwell performs his solo soundtrack to the 1962 Harry Smith film “Heaven and Earth Magic” in the UK for the first time. Negativland play the UK for the first time in eight years, and 2nd Gen for the first time anywhere since 2009. The Soft Pink Truth, a Matmos offshoot, makes its first UK appearance since 2008, while M.C. Schmidt and Obel Feldi, another Matmos-related project, make their UK debut. Sunroof, the duo of Mute Records founder Daniel Miller and producer Gareth Jones, add a rare live outing to the bill. Githead – Colin Newman of Wire, Malka Spiegel of Minimal Compact and Robin Rimbaud aka Scanner – reunite after a 13-year hiatus, with Newman and Spiegel also performing separately as Immersion. Rimbaud joins Vicki Bennett of People Like Us and Carl Stone for a rare live outing of their trio project Mischievous Misappropriators. As previously announced, JG Thirlwell’s Foetus set is a European exclusive drawing on his 2026 album “HALT” and earlier material, presented as a large orchestral format for only the second time and his first UK appearance as Foetus in over 25 years. Lustmord plays the UK for the first time in almost a decade. Shadowlands is co-founded by David Sefton, former Head of Artistic Development at the Royal Festival Hall/Southbank Centre in London, who originated the Meltdown festival in 1993. Co-founder Gerard Myers stated the festival’s line-up was built around artists he and Sefton wanted to see together rather than genre or era, adding that some acts agreed to reform once approached. Sefton described the goal as identifying “the most exciting line-up of the most adventurous music ever made” and then booking it. The festival has 450 tickets available, including a three-monthly-payment option, with on-site accommodation bookable now via the official site. Canterbury’s proximity to London, mainland Europe and major airports is positioned as part of the event’s appeal. Shadowlands 2027 full line-up Foetus (20-piece chamber orchestra), Lustmord, Test Dept., Clock DVA, The Wolfgang Press, Portion Control, :Zoviet*France, Warrington-Runcorn New Town Development Plan, Regis (feat. Liam Andrews), People Like Us, These New Puritans, Matmos, Årabrot, Hula, Barry Adamson, Sunroof, JG Thirlwell (solo), Negativland, Globo, The Soft Pink Truth, Carl Stone, 2nd Gen, Mischievous Misappropriators, Monosum, M.C. Schmidt and Obel Feldi, Githead, Immersion, and Rangelova (DJ). About Shadowlands Shadowlands is a new boutique international festival taking place across four days at the Gulbenkian Arts Centre on the University of Kent campus in Canterbury, England, from 1 to 4 July 2027. It was co-founded by David Sefton, former Head of Artistic Development at the Royal Festival Hall/Southbank Centre in London and originator of the Meltdown festival, together with Gerard Myers. The festival describes itself as “The Outside Of Everything,” positioning its programme around artists spanning industrial, electronic, avant-garde and experimental music rather than a single genre or era. Beyond concerts, the festival includes talks, Q&As and film screenings across three venues. Several headline acts connect to Side-Line’s own coverage history: Clock DVA issued a remastered “Sensorium” single ahead of its “Thirst” 45th-anniversary reissue earlier in 2026, and its member Adi Newton also performs at Shadowlands as T.A.G.C. The Canterbury debut follows a first-wave announcement of 19 acts on 2 July, expanded to 35 with the additions confirmed on 10 September.

items.body: Review by XixoTheRock — "Universo rojo"s social media accounts have been dead since 2021, the band, located in Vi�a delMar, apparently has no plans of coming back together in the near future, I must admit, that just asthere's a mystery around this LP (I will later tell you why!), it remains a mystery why they justdissapeared from social media for 5 years now!The band hands us this record in a silver platter, claiming that it is a conceptual record, indeed Icould see where they are going, the way the album sounds is overall telling of the nature of therecord itself, yet, and now I'll tell you the mystery, there's almost no lyrics! It's a semi fullyinstrumental album, with the only spoken sections being some indigenous like chants on the secondtrack "Visi�n planetaria de los tiempos", which seem to be in a native American language, I'd say itmost likely is Mapudungun, however, these chants and lyrics have no subtitles available on thedescription of the track (at least on platforms such as Spotify), and the singer seems to beuncredited, ladies and gentlemen this is the mystery I told you about! What do these lyrics meanexactly, and who sang them? It's captivating how a detail so simple can imply so many things!Musically wise, the music delivers an interesting experience which mixes krautrock with psychedelicrock and some elements of Zeuhl. Speaking of Zeuhl, it seems to be one of the main genres the bandlooks up to, as their publicly available playlist is dominated by bands such as Magma and Weidorje,as well as kasutrock acts like Popol Vuh and Amon D��l II, interestingly enough, we find some ratherodd influences that stand out in their playlist, like the extreme doom metal band Sunnata. Beinghighly influenced by classic experimental genres characterized by their use of symphonicinstrumentation, tape effects, spiritual topics and repetitiveness, "Impermanencia" is full ofsynthetizers, tape loops, repetitions of bass lines and riffs and a very hypotonic, spiral like windof textures and noises, all contributing to the creation of pieces which feel less like music andmore akin to a state of trance and meditation, albeit a very chaotic one. Each composition feelsvery much like the previous one, with little variation in the state it indices on the listener, thisoverall calmer and more meditative approach to music, will appeal to those invested in ambient andkraut, but won't satisfy those who prefer Zeuhl or more expressive, grandiose symphonic rock. The album has a lot of influences, although most can't be felt, but when it shows the signs, itsounds great! I'd like to point out that I was fairly dissapointed, as I was promised a magnum opus,a masterclass for the genre and most of the times, the record feels like an experiment halfway doneor a very relaxing jamming session.The musicianship is good enough, you can feel that each instrument was recorded separately and thenpieced together with the others, they are talented players but you can't really feel much chemistrybetween the parts that make the music, if you add this to what I previously stated, you get the fullpicture : this record is much more like something "Stars of the lid" would do if they went a littlemore experimental and not something that comes out of the chaotic mess of Zeuhl or the mathematicsof krautrock.My biggest issue with this record is the production, which is straight up unbearable...this recordsounds muddy, grainy, blurry and inconsistent, because yes, some tracks have good production and theother an awful one, and the difference is so noticeable it makes it uncomfortable to listen to. Thedrums can't even be heard most of the time, a record so inspired by krautrock should have a veryclear rhythmic direction and presence, which can't be heard through at least half of the record.I give it 2 stars because it's an interesting record to dig into and because of how hypnotic anduseful for meditation it is, but musically itself, I don't really see much to highlight...it'salmost as if it were an experiment that was never properly finished, this is sad because thisproject had so much potential.
items._genre: psychedelic rock / space rock / krautrock / zeuhl
items._cn_summary: 智利乐队Universo Rojo的第二张专辑以半器乐方式展开概念叙事，融合了Krautrock的循环律动、Psychedelic Rock的音色质感与Zeuhl的奇异结构。专辑中穿插了疑似Mapudungun的原住民吟唱，但未提供歌词字幕，歌手也未署名，留下神秘的文化与美学空白。音乐层面大量使用合成器、磁带循环、低音线条与节奏的重复堆叠，营造出冥想与恍惚交织的氛围，但整体变化有限，结构上更接近半完成的实验或即兴录音。评论者期待中的杰作未能完全实现，但乐队在音色纹理和氛围构建上展现了一定实力。专辑对Magma、Popol Vuh、Amon Düül II等经典实验乐队有明显致敬，同时吸收了Sunnata等极端Doom元素。作为拉丁美洲小厂牌发行，作品带有南美原住民文化的独特视角，对偏爱实验与跨界融合的听众具有一定吸引力。

items.body: California duo Antania release the single and video “33”, the first taste of their new album The Unholy 33, due 16 October 2026 via Argonauta Records. The digital album follows, with physical CD and vinyl editions to be detailed later. Antania, the project of Doc Luna and Kali Mortem, build “33” entirely without conventional guitars or bass, relying instead on synthesizers, distorted textures and machine-like rhythms. The duo describe their sound as avant-garde black metal filtered through industrial and experimental electronics, citing Dødheimsgard, Mysticum and Thorns alongside the dark electronic legacies of Skinny Puppy and Ministry as reference points. “The Unholy 33” runs eleven tracks: “33”, “DVHM3R”, “Sn0wAnGeL”, “Gloomzday”, “ThUgG33”, “Cykl0pZ”, “Flies”, “AntVniV”, “Frazzledrip”, “Kultz” and “HEarSe”. Following the album’s release, Doc Luna and Kali Mortem head to Asia in support, joining Swedish extreme metal act The Crown for dates in the UAE, Japan and South Korea, followed by an appearance alongside Evergrey in India. About Antania Antania is the Californian duo of Doc Luna and Kali Mortem. The project began as a doom-bass act, releasing the debut album “Lividity” in 2023 before signing with Triad Records later that year. Antania supported Psyclon Nine on a 2024 European tour alongside Devil M. “The Unholy 33” marks the duo’s move to Argonauta Records and a shift toward the avant-garde industrial black metal sound built entirely from electronics.
items._genre: avant-garde black metal / industrial / electronic / experimental
items._cn_summary: 加州二人组Antania发布新专辑《The Unholy 33》的首支单曲及MV，专辑定于2026年10月由Argonauta Records发行。整张作品完全摒弃传统吉他与贝斯，仅依靠合成器、失真音色层叠与机械感节奏构建声响，自定位为前卫黑金属经由工业与实验电子的过滤。参考谱系涵盖Dødheimsgard、Mysticum、Thorns等极端金属先驱，以及Skinny Puppy与Ministry的暗黑电子遗产。专辑收录十首作品，风格在粗砺噪音与冷峻电子氛围间切换。发行后将随The Crown赴阿联酋、日本、韩国巡演，并与Evergrey同台亮相印度。乐队此前以doom-bass项目起步，此作标志着其向全电子驱动的工业黑金属转型。

items.body: FOURSCHER Festival returns to Club From Hell in Erfurt, Germany, on 7 and 8 November 2026, with nine acts spanning EBM, dark electro, rhythmic noise and ritual electronics: Snog, Black Lung, Individual Totem, Mildreda, This Morn’ Omina, Heimstatt Yipotash, Polykoptr, KIFOTH and Manipulation. Having attended the festival twice, in 2024 and 2025, what stood out both times was less any single performance than the combination of a carefully selected programme, an open audience and the sense that organisers Danny Hildebrandt and Andreas Schubert were personally invested in how people experienced the weekend. That impression carries into the 2026 edition, where the nine acts are connected less by genre than by a shared refusal to treat the existing vocabulary of industrial and electronic music as sufficient on its own: some dismantle it, some stretch it toward ritual or techno, some return to it after decades, and some use familiar EBM structures to ask questions that have little to do with genre loyalty. The clearest example is the pairing of Snog and Black Lung, both projects of David Thrussell. Snog works through legible structures, songs, hooks, slogans and satire, using the dancefloor to examine consumerism, obedience and political absurdity. Black Lung strips away that accessibility for harder, darker and more experimental electronic forms. Their FOURSCHER appearances are billed as their only European shows of 2026; a new Black Lung album, “Ordo Ab Chao,” is due shortly before the festival. Individual Totem bring an electro industrial catalogue reaching back to the 1990s, including records such as “S.E.T.I.,” “Mothfly,” “Kyria 13” and “Electrostatic,” with live appearances rare enough that the Erfurt date carries weight of its own. Mildreda’s context is more immediate: “Realities,” released 28 August, pushes Jan Dewulf’s work into a space where dark electronic abrasion sits alongside more emotional exposure than the genre typically allows, while retaining the project’s Canadian EBM and Belgian electronic lineage. This Morn’ Omina arrive in their thirtieth year with new release “Vestiges,” which frames three decades as continuity of practice rather than a retrospective; the project’s rhythm-driven material has always worked to alter a listener’s sense of duration and physical orientation rather than simply carry songs. Heimstatt Yipotash’s 2026 album “Abyss” draws on the physical conditions of the deep sea, pressure, isolation, cold and downward movement, as both imagery and compositional logic, moving between aggressive electro, rhythm noise and more cinematic passages. Polykoptr comes from the wider Amnistia orbit and the Leipzig electronic scene, presented here on its own terms rather than as an extension of that name. The Slovak project KIFOTH released “Artificial Territory” in June 2026, reconnecting earlier KIFOTH material with contemporary EBM production. Manipulation return after close to three decades, with “Feel The Same” remembered as a small club hit from the project’s earlier run. Line-up and practical information FOURSCHER Festival 2026 takes place at Club From Hell, Flughafenstraße 41, 99092 Erfurt, Germany, on 7 November (19:00-03:00) and 8 November (13:00-18:00). The line-up: Snog, Black Lung, Individual Totem, Mildreda, This Morn’ Omina, Heimstatt Yipotash, Polykoptr, KIFOTH and Manipulation. Tickets are priced at €70 for the weekend or €40 for a day ticket; electronic tickets are available, with printed tickets held at the box office on request.

items.body: Catherine Ringer, vocalist, songwriter, and co-founder of French new wave duo Les Rita Mitsouko, has died at age 68. Her children announced her death in a statement to AFP, confirming that she died from cancer on the night of September 14, 2026. With her partner in music and life, Fred Chichin, Ringer made pop music feel large enough to accommodate almost anything: punk impatience, funk, cabaret, electronic experimentation, and the expressive possibilities of French chanson. A song could be funny, sensual, disconcerting, and profoundly sad within the same few minutes. Ringer gave each feeling its own physical presence, singing with a freedom that made conventional ideas of good taste seem rather timid. Born on October 18, 1957, in Suresnes, near Paris, she was the daughter of painter Sam Ringer, a Polish-born Jewish Holocaust survivor, and an architect mother. She left school at 15 and pursued an artistic education through theatre, music, and dance. Among the formative figures in her life was Argentine dancer and choreographer Marcia Moretto, who became her teacher and collaborator. Those years onstage helped establish the connection between movement and voice that would distinguish her work with Les Rita Mitsouko. Nostalgie’s biography documents her early performances and work with Moretto. Ringer met Chichin in 1979, beginning a partnership that would carry them from the Paris underground to international recognition. Their self-titled 1984 debut, recorded with Conny Plank, introduced a group whose appetite for experiment came with a formidable instinct for melody. As Coilhouse’s retrospective observed, Ringer’s background in avant-garde theatre remained visible in the duo’s performances and videos. Marcia Baïla became their breakthrough. Written in remembrance of Moretto following her death from cancer, it joined the exhilaration of dance to the shock of losing someone whose life had been devoted to movement. Its popularity carried that private grief into public celebration. The song offers an especially poignant way to remember Ringer now: affection, anger, and delight sharing the same space, with no easy separation between them. Directed by Philippe Gautier, the music video for Marcia Baïla gave the song an equally extravagant visual life, with costumes by Jean Paul Gaultier and Thierry Mugler. Watch the video below. The duo’s collaboration with Tony Visconti on The No Comprendo in 1986 brought Andy, C’est comme ça, and Les Histoires d’A. The album won at the 1987 Victoires de la Musique, as did Jean-Baptiste Mondino’s video for C’est comme ça. These songs remain an excellent introduction to Ringer’s range: the teasing insistence of Andy, the sharp attack of C’est comme ça, and the ease with which she could make a repeated phrase feel like an argument, an invitation, or a joke. Their creative world extended well beyond records. Jean-Luc Godard included the duo at work in his 1987 film Soigne ta droite, while collaborations brought them together with fellow musical eccentrics. Sparks joined them for Singing in the Shower, from 1988’s Marc & Robert, a meeting of artists who understood how much pleasure could be found in pop’s peculiar corners. Later, Iggy Pop appeared on My Love Is Bad, preserved alongside their other collaborations in the band’s collected catalogue. The apparent playfulness could also carry terrible knowledge. Le Petit Train addressed the deportation trains of the Holocaust, a history bound closely to her father’s survival. Its video, filmed in Bombay, placed Ringer amid exuberant dancing while the words described people being carried toward their deaths. The tension between the music’s invitation and the lyric’s meaning remains deeply unsettling. She understood how a familiar pleasure could open an audience to something painful. Chichin died from cancer in 2007, aged 53, the year Les Rita Mitsouko released Variéty. Ringer continued performing their songs while building a solo catalogue that included Ring n’ Roll in 2011 and Chroniques et fantaisies in 2017. With Plaza Francia, alongside Gotan Project’s Eduardo Makaroff and Christoph H. Müller, she explored tango on 2014’s A New Tango Song Book. Her later work also returned to the intimacy of spoken language. In L’Érotisme de vivre, she performed the poetry of Alice Mendelson, accompanied by pianist Grégoire Hetzel under the direction of Mauro Gioia. The scale had changed, but the curiosity remained: another writer, another setting, another way to give words a body. Ringer leaves music full of appetite and contradiction, open to beauty without becoming polite about it. She made eccentricity feel generous, something an audience could participate in. Our thoughts are with her family, friends, collaborators, and everyone who found freedom in her voice. Follow Catherine Ringer: Instagram Facebook Follow Les Rita Mitsouko Instagram YouTube Bandcamp The post Catherine Ringer, the Extraordinary Voice of Les Rita Mitsouko, Has Passed Away at 68 appeared first on Post-Punk.com.

items._cn_summary: 本文为法国新浪潮双人组Les Rita Mitsouko主唱Catherine Ringer的讣告式回顾。她与音乐及人生伴侣Fred Chichin合作，将朋克躁动、放克韵律、电子实验与法语香颂熔于一炉，以戏剧化的舞台表现力模糊了高雅与通俗的边界。文章追溯了她的艺术成长——从早年的剧场与舞蹈训练，到与制作人Conny Plank和Tony Visconti的合作，记录了1984年同名首作与1986年《The No Comprendo》等里程碑。代表作《Marcia Baila》将私人丧痛与公共庆典并置，体现了她声音中戏谑、愤怒、柔情与感伤并存的特质。文中还涉及Jean Paul Gaultier与Thierry Mugler的服装设计、Jean-Luc Godard的电影合作，展现了二人超越音乐的广阔艺术世界。

items.body: A short intro on "Sculpting Silence" The nature of art is to make you stop you in your tracks, to stop doing what you're doing and thinking, and to start using your senses, your eyes and ears, sometimes your touch and smell to be surprised, to be confronted with the unexpected, to admire, to see things differently. We will have a short series of music that we describe as "s culpting silence ", music in which sound is used like the black lines of a pen in zen art, a few strokes that capture the essence on a white canvas. And the first album in the series explicitly refers to the Zen concepts of ' Mu ' and ' Shin ' : " The term combines the kanji Mu (nothingness) and Shin (mind or spirit), and is often translated as “no-mind.” It refers to a state of consciousness free from fear, anger, or ego—where action arises naturally and without obstruction. In musical terms, this becomes a space where sound is not forced or premeditated, but emerges with clarity and immediacy ", we read in the liner notes. So the few strokes on a white canvas - on 'nothingness' - are like the ripples on a still pond, the barely visible effect of the slightest breeze. Here are some descriptions I found on the value of the colour 'white' in Zen art, comparable to silence in music. In Zen art, white is not merely a blank background or an empty void. It represents 'ma' (negative space), functioning as living breath, silence, and the infinite potential from which all forms emerge and return. The unpainted white paper or silk is an active, essential presence equal to the black ink strokes. Zen painting uses intentional emptiness, asymmetry, and abbreviated forms to point toward direct seeing rather than decoration. Blank space is not “nothing”; it functions as breath, silence, and the field in which forms appear and dissolve. Common motifs—enso, bamboo, landscapes, and solitary figures—teach non-attachment and ordinary clarity. I also found some sayings about listening. "Listening stops with the ears, the mind stops with recognition, but spirit is empty and waits on all things." "What is this mind? Who is hearing these sounds? ... What is it that hears?" "The quieter you become, the more you can hear." Now about the album. The cover art is bizarre, to say the least: a cigarette-smoking armour seated on a toilet in a hilly landscape. It's in bad taste in my opinion, and not because of the toilet, but also because it does not truly reflect the nature of the music. It's a surreal digital artwork created by Aki Karano (also known as Akis Karanos) a visual artist and experimental musician, based in Greece. In retrospect, it looks familiar when you see the likeness with the traditional Japanese drawings of monks contemplating the world, and also seen from the back. There may be a reference, or it might just be a coincidence. Admitted, the monk is not smoking and not wearing an armour, and he's contemplating a circle and not a square, yet it might be a more modern, more surreal rendition of the same experience. Now really about the album. Both Susana Santos Silva on trumpet and Vasco Trilla on percussion explore the boundaries and sonic potential of their respective instruments, creating ringing tones, whistles, droplets, swooshes, rumbles, gurgles, swishes and many more sounds without name or description. The album begins quietly, with uncommon sounds cautiously flirting with silence—touching it slowly and gently, as if aware of its fragility. The result is a kind of soft intensity, with no obvious path or predetermined concept beyond the simple act of producing small fragments of sound and welcoming their clarity, their unexpectedness, and the ways in which they interact. This is music that has nothing to prove. It does not seek to impress, move, or even necessarily engage a listener or an audience. It exists simply for its own sake: to be savoured, appreciated, and perhaps approached with the same state of mind as the artists themselves—with no attachment and no anticipation. Such an experience can only emerge from going beyond the expected, allowing the music to develop organically and naturally, as if arising from nothingness. Contrary to the liner notes, I would recommend simply listening, rather than reflecting while you listen. Let yourself become part of the experience. Be there in the moment. Both Santos Silva and Trilla are masters of their art. They share a remarkable sensitivity and an innovative ability to draw sounds from their instruments that are rarely heard, while employing a wide range of techniques and tools to sustain the listener’s attention. As with much improvised music, the album may surprise you on a first listen, but it reveals more of itself with each return. Be the music. Listen and download from Bandcamp . Email This BlogThis! Share to X Share to Facebook
items._cn_summary: 这是《Sculpting Silence》系列的开篇之作，由Susana Santos Silva与Vasco Trilla演绎，以禅宗“无心”概念为核心展开音乐实验。两位音乐家以极简笔触勾勒声响，如同水墨画中留白所承载的呼吸与潜能——声音不刻意预设，而是在静默中自然涌现。专辑将东方哲学中“间”的概念转化为听觉体验，每一处声响犹如投入静潭的涟漪，轻微却清晰。乐评以大量篇幅阐述禅宗美学中白色作为“活的存在”之意涵，并将其类比为音乐中的沉默本身。封面由希腊视觉艺术家Aki Karano创作，以数字绘画呈现一位抽烟的武士僧侣坐于山间马桶的超现实场景，刻意与传统日本禅僧冥想图形成反差。乐评指出此封面虽风格诡异，与音乐内在气质存在张力，却可能在反讽层面构成对当代禅修语境的一种戏谑回应。

items.body:
A key presence on the New York scene over the past 30 years, trumpeter, composer, arranger, and bandleader Steven Bernstein has immersed himself in such a wide array of music with his bands Sexmob, Millennial Territory Orchestra, Diaspora Soul, Universal Melody Brass Band, Spanish Fly, Blue Campfire, and the Butler-Bernstein Hot 9 that his output defies easy categorization. A former member of The Lounge Lizards and Levon Helm’s Midnight Ramble Band, Bernstein has also composed works for film, theater, and dance in addition to doing arrangements for a diverse list of artists, including Lou Reed, Lee “Scratch” Perry, Allen Toussaint, Marianne Faithfull, Linda Ronstadt, Rufus Wainwright, Darlene Love, Mario Pavone, Bill Frisell, and John Lurie. His lengthy list of sideman credits includes appearances on recent recordings by Laurie Anderson (Heart of a Dog), Roswell Rudd (Trombone for Lovers), Mostly Other People Do the Killing (Loafer’s Hollow), Antony and the Johnsons (Turning), and Nels Cline (Lovers). He also continues to perform with Ray Anderson’s Pocket Brass Band, Omaha Diner, and the Kamikaze Ground Crew.

Born in Berkeley, California, Bernstein moved to New York in 1978. By 1990 he had joined The Lounge Lizards, appearing on the group’s 1991 release Live in Berlin (Intuition). Shortly before that, in 1988 he formed the trio Spanish Fly with slide guitarist Dave Tronzo and tuba virtuoso Marcus Rojas. By 1995, producer Hal Willner, a fan of Spanish Fly, enlisted Bernstein as arranger for the soundtrack to Robert Altman’s film Kansas City, which led to collaborations on numerous other Willner projects, including tributes to Bill Withers, Doc Pomus, and Leonard Cohen, among many others.

In 1996, Bernstein formed Sexmob with saxophonist Briggan Krauss, bassist Tony Scherr, and drummer Kenny Wollesen. It remains his primary vehicle for exploring the slide trumpet, a rare instrument that he picked up in a Woodstock guitar shop back in 1977. Over two decades of recording, the group has put their singular stamp on an eclectic list of tunes by the likes of Leadbelly, John Barry, Hoagy Carmichael, Paul McCartney, Duke Ellington, Prince, Kurt Cobain, the Rolling Stones, James Brown, Count Basie, Professor Longhair, and Nino Rota. The group’s latest album, in its 20th anniversary year, is Cultural Capital, the first Sexmob recording to feature all original compositions.

From 1999 to 2008, Bernstein contributed four recordings to John Zorn’s Radical Jewish Culture series on his Tzadik label – 1999’s Diaspora Soul (featuring members of The Lounge Lizards and Sexmob), 2002’s Diaspora Blues (featuring Sam Rivers), 2004’s Diaspora Hollywood (inspired by classic film composers and West Coast cool jazz), and 2008’s Diaspora Suite (a homecoming recorded with Bay Area musicians). Each project combined traditional cantorial songs and elements of jazz, blues, and rock.

Bernstein’s Millennial Territory Orchestra debuted with 2006’s MTO, Vol. 1, which featured large ensemble interpretations of songs by Stevie Wonder, Prince, and the Grateful Dead, as well as Benny Moten and Charlie Johnson and His Paradise Band. They followed with 2008’s We Are MTO, which included renditions of tunes by Fats Waller, Don Redman, Count Basie, and the Beatles. Their 2011 recording, MTO Plays Sly, was a tribute to the music of Sly & The Family Stone and featured the late P-Funk keyboardist Bernie Worrell along with guest vocalists.

In 2012, Bernstein joined up with New Orleans piano master Henry Butler in the retro-flavored Butler, Bernstein and the Hot 9. Their critically acclaimed 2014 Impulse! debut, Viper’s Drag, featured spirited renditions of Fats Waller’s title track along with tunes by Jelly Roll Morton and originals by Butler. The restlessly creative Bernstein continues to juggle several working bands. During a recent residency at The Stone in NYC, he performed with Sexmob, Millennial Territory Orchestra, Spanish Fly, Blue Campfire, and Universal Melody Brass Band.

Bernstein’s latest album is ResoNation Trio/Ultra Resonance (Royal Potato Family). In the liner notes, Bernstein mentions being enchanted by Burning Spear’s Garvey’s Ghost (Island, 1976) back in 1981, only realizing years later that it was a dub version of Marcus Garvey, Burning Spear’s Island release from the previous year. Since then, Bernstein has wanted to record an acoustic jazz trio album and have the results remade as a dub album. The first half of the release, ResoNation Trio, features Bernstein on trumpets, Scott Colley on contrabass, and Nasheet Waits on drums. To challenge himself, Bernstein eschews his main axe (slide trumpet) for this session and instead plays regular valve trumpet, G trumpet, and flugelhorn. The second half is called Ultra Resonance and features the first session tapes remixed and rearranged in dub fashion by longtime producer Scotty Hard, who also adds various keyboards, samples, and percussion to the mix. The former date is as spartan as the latter is dense, yet the two recordings (different though they are in concept and execution), are inextricably linked. I interviewed Bernstein in the summer of 2026, shortly after the release of ResoNation Trio/Ultra Resonance.

* * *

Troy Collins: You’ve been touring with Laurie Anderson the past few years, as documented by the recently released Let X = X (Nonesuch), which features Sexmob as Anderson’s backing band. What has it been like interpreting and rearranging her tunes for Sexmob, especially since Sexmob (in)famously doesn’t typically use pre-arranged tunes and/or setlists? And perhaps more importantly, how did this particular collaboration come about and what is working with Anderson herself like?

Steven Bernstein: Playing with Laurie has been a life-changing experience. She is completely about creation, being in the moment, acting on every inspiration, trying every idea and having fun. Her work ethic is legendary. Her ability to transform an audience is mastery. So being around her and that energy is just a powerful and positive situation. Even though a “show” is basically set once Laurie has decided on it (we are touring a completely different concert, different songs, different stories, different visuals, and a different “theme”) we/she are constantly making changes. Every show day we are at the theatre by 2:00 pm (she gets there at 11:00 am to start working with the lighting director) and we run every piece, whether a new idea comes from Laurie, me, another member of the band, a random sound that makes Laurie say “What’s that? Let’s try that in ‘___’.” Every idea is entertained and often added to the show.

The story of how this all started is beautiful. I’ve been around Laurie and known her at a distance for a long time, but the first time we really worked closely was doing Hal Willner’s Leonard Cohen show in Brighton in 2004. I arranged two songs for her, “The Guest” and “If It Be Your Will.” At Hal’s memorial she wanted to do Lou Reed’s “Gassed and Stoked.” I brought an arrangement that sounded just like the record and we played it through. She turned to me and said, “that sounds great, but I had another idea, I have this new loop” and she starts activating the loop with her violin bowing. It was a very “Laurie-style” loop: rhythmic, sonic, and not in 4/4 time. Tony and Kenny just drop in and start playing. It was grooving and effortless from the first sound. Laurie ended up testing positive for Covid and was unable to play the memorial, but a week later she calls and says how much fun she had playing with us. She said, “I’ve never had that feeling playing music” and that Warners is re-releasing her records and she was thinking of revisiting her older material (which she had never done), and asked would Sexmob play with her? You know my answer.

TC: Since you mentioned him, I’d be remiss to not ask about your years working with Hal Willner. The man’s various artist projects were significant touchstones in my development as a listener. I know he was a big fan of Spanish Fly – is that how you first met? And how did you become his go-to arranger for so many of his projects?

SB: I heard Hal’s Nino Rota record the summer of 1981 while visiting back home in Berkeley. Peter Engelhart, the legendary metal percussion maker played it for me (his daughters are some of my oldest and best friends). It changed my DNA! After that it became a thing. Who is Hal Willner? Where is Hal Willner? I did Night Music with Karen Mantler in 1989. I also played with Carla Bley, Bootsy, and Allen Toussaint on that show. Hal came up to me and said that he was a fan of Spanish Fly, that he’d been coming to our gigs at the Knitting Factory (lurking in the back I’m sure). He gave me his number and said that he would love to help us in any way he could. That led to him producing the first Spanish Fly record (on Knitting Factory records). It is a great Hal Willner production. Hal and I had very similar musical loves and ideas about music, he believed in me and kept offering me amazing opportunities. That led to a 25-year relationship. He could ask me to arrange for Elton John, Bill Frisell, Nick Cave, Lou Reed, Courtney Love, Robert Altman, Marshall Allan, U2 – it was always magic and natural. When I met him, it was pre-internet, and I would keep a pad of paper next to me during our phone conversations. His references could be Ernie Kovacs, Rahsaan, Allan Ginsberg, Martin Denny, Dorothy Parker, Anne Waldman, The Three Stooges, Gregory Corso, Fellini ... I did my best to keep up and learned a lot.

TC: Talking about Willner reminds me that you’ve done arrangements for more people than I can list, and the stylistic variety of artists is staggering. I’m curious if there’s ever been any job you feel you couldn’t or wouldn’t do?

To clarify, the beautiful thing about music is that someone else can take a song that seems unsalvageable and make something new from it that the original author may not have ever suspected was possible. Having just listened to a recent interview with Bill Frisell, I was reminded of his rendition of Madonna’s “Live To Tell,” which transforms what I would consider to be a lightweight pop song into a rhapsodic epic.

You are obviously capable of the same magic, but I wonder, have there ever been offers that you’ve refused based on the material or direction that someone wanted to go with it? Have you ever encountered a song that you felt was simply unredeemable?

SB: Well, there’s a funny story from about 8 years ago, at the beginning of Trump’s 1st term. It was a slow time (as often is the case for freelance workers) and I got an email from someone about arranging/producing some songs. The guy is a Sexmob fan, knows my work with Hal, and he has written some protest songs, tells me he thinks he can get Bono to sing on them, etc. He is not a professional musician, but this is his passion. He also has a vision of a performance piece situation, where the song is played while the listener goes down the “golden elevator” and walks somewhere else. We agree to a fee and he sends me the demo. He is playing rudimentary chords on the piano, and sings one verse, one chorus – it’s about 25 seconds. I call him and ask if there is more, he says no that’s the song. I explain that songs usually have a second or third verse, maybe a bridge, but he says no this is the song. I explain to him that it’s about 25 seconds, and if he wants it to work the way he is envisioning, (going down the elevator and walking) it needs to be at least 3 minutes long. He says, “Well do that Sexmob thing.” I talk to my wife and tell her that I don’t know if I can do this and she says “I thought you said you can make music out of anything.” So, I did and it ended up very cool!

TC: Well then, the obvious follow-up question to that is – did Bono sing on it?

SB: NO. A total pipe dream!

TC: Since we’ve been talking about arranging, I assume nothing is off limits in your own bands regarding your original tunes. Are there any pieces specifically written for say Sexmob, Millennial Territory Orchestra, or Spanish Fly that don’t translate as well from one band to the other, or do you compose your pieces so that any of your bands can perform them?

SB: Each piece is written not only for the band, but specifically for the players in each band. So, there hasn’t been much crossover. There is a piece I wrote as a commission during the pandemic that I played with Sexmob and MTO, but it really worked better as an MTO piece. But the very last phrase (the kicker) of the MTO end of night theme came from a Spanish Fly composition!

TC: Let’s move on to your new album. Your latest release for Royal Potato Family, ResoNation Trio/Ultra Resonance present two very different facets of your artistry – the former title finds you playing on valve trumpet and flugelhorn (instead of the ubiquitous slide trumpet) accompanied by bassist Scott Colley and drummer Nasheet Waits, while the later features Scotty Hard remixing the trio. How did this project come about and when did you first meet and work with Scotty Hard? It seems to me your working relationship with Hard goes all the way back to the very first Sexmob album, 1998’s Din of Inequity.

SB: This project came about because of a grant from the Shifting Foundation. The idea of creating original music with the orchestration of valve trumpet, acoustic bass, and drum set has been a dream of mine for a very long time. This particular vibrational intersection is not widely used, so the unknown possibilities are vast. On a musical/improvisational/technical level it has a very specific set of challenges, and it has taken me this long to feel ready to undertake this long-held desire. Scott Colley and Nasheet were always the musicians I wanted to do this with; I have known them both a long time, and they are veteran masters of spontaneous composition. Another long-held dream has been to create a dub version of an improvisatory instrumental record. I heard Garvey’s Ghost in 1981, and it changed my DNA. Once I started making my own records, I was just waiting for the right opportunity ... and this was it. The trio record is purely conversational and in the moment; back porch music with unlimited harmonic and structural possibilities. The time spent on this record was the decades of playing and writing that preceded it. Ultra Resonance is a mirror image, in that Scott creates his pieces layer by layer, adding and subtracting sounds and rhythms – it takes weeks to build a track.

When I first started playing in The Lounge Lizards with Michael Blake on tenor, Scotty started coming to hang; he was a friend of Michael’s from Vancouver. The first session we did with him was for a Justin Warfield record on Quincy Jones’ label Qwest. It was produced by Prince Paul (I am a huge fan of De La Soul). Scotty wrote the horn chart and engineered. Scotty went on to record and produce the first four Sexmob records. I was already doing fast cuts and dropouts live, but Scotty’s mixes/arrangements shaped the sound of the band.

TC: Having just listened to Sexotica (Thirsty Ear, 2006), your collaborative effort with the production duo known as GoodandEvil (Danny Blume and Chris Castagno), I’m curious how that experience was compared to your similar efforts with Scotty Hard? How does GoodandEvil’s working method differ from Hard’s and what are your thoughts on the different outcomes?

SB: Regarding the two albums/processes – they were fundamentally different as working methods and outcomes. We went into Sexotica (which got a Grammy nomination) with the idea of creating a project that was half acoustic and half electronic. Sexmob went on and recorded all the compositions (two of them being loose jams with input from Danny Blume). Then we did a full day of overdubs with Kenny: wood percussion, metal percussion, bird whistles, and gongs. Then GoodandEvil did their magic. Some pieces skewed more acoustic, some more electronic. The idea was an even balance overall.

With Ultra Resonance Scott was given all the tracks (20 songs). The first track he made, “Titano,” was a piece that’s not on the trio record, but I felt it would be a good piece for Scotty to put his magic on. I figured he would do a “remix” of it, but he rewrote the bass line and created a brand-new piece (natch). After that it was just letting Scott experiment and follow his muse. We had mapped out a series of “zones” we wanted the pieces to be in, but everything Scotty created was totally unexpected. Part of this was the idea of intentional experimentation – on both of our parts. For me it was the idea of the acoustic record, for Scotty it was some new boxes/plug-ins that he had recently received, and the idea of not going back to his tried-and-true techniques. Also, with Sexotica I was not involved in their process, but with Scotty I would hang in the studio once the “track” was created, and was involved in arranging process (Scott claims I had 3 good ideas, I’d say more like 7.6).

As far as my thoughts on the outcomes – two singular recordings that I believe are unlike anything else in the modern recording world. I’m proud of that.

TC: Switching gears slightly (towards acoustic sounds), you’re a fan of vintage horns. I’m assuming that there are certain models you never take on tour and some that you take on the road more frequently? What are the criteria for those distinctions? And what about the slide trumpet? I’m not familiar with anyone else playing one, so where and when did you ever find one?

SB: Vintage trumpets aren’t an issue on the road. I just use the horn best suited for the music. The horn I used touring with Levon Helm was a handmade Chicago Benge from 1947. That was a horn that could project over a five-piece horn section and two electric guitars. It had amazing response and Levon could feel my beat matching his. That’s not what I need with Laurie Anderson!

Regarding the slide trumpet – I found my first horn in a guitar store in Woodstock in 1977 when I was attending Creative Music Studio. When I started Sexmob 30 years ago my old friend (and master repairman) Dick Akright in Oakland (who I met in 6th grade) built the horn I use. It’s one a kind! I’ve collected almost every brand of slide trumpet over the years, though they are not as playable as my horn.

The first horn was $25, at the time (mid-70s) and many trumpet players had one because they were cheap and easily available.

TC: Speaking of Levon Helm, what was it like working with Helm and how did that relationship come about?

SB: This is a long story. I knew Levon had been having “rent party” gigs at the barn. Tony Scherr had done some, and Erik Lawrence did as well. Levon was in danger of losing the barn, as this was a last-ditch attempt to raise some money and also make some music. Erik had invited me to play a few times, and there was a Saturday where I was available (I often did a wedding on Saturday, as I was raising a family, and those gigs paid the bills). Anyway, they mention a few songs Levon might want to do (no Band songs) and said come up early because we might rehearse. We got up there and Levon didn’t come out, so I sat with a boombox and learned a few more songs that Levon “might want to do.” It was a nice chill hang up there, and when it became clear that there was not going to be any rehearsing, I told Erik Lawrence “Don’t play what I play. You just play what you hear, and I’ll play what I hear.” That way we were both free to react to the music. We were playing with Olabelle, and Levon just walked up and got behind the drums. It was the most natural improvisation/spontaneous composition. Levon didn’t know my name, had never seen me before, just smiled at me and told me what he needed with his drum fills. It was magic, and in true Levon form, he put a song from that night on one of his CD’s. Pure improvisation – we had never met!

As far as working with him – it was some of the most magic, swinging, joyous, pure music I have ever had the opportunity to create. He taught me so much about playing in time, playing melody, playing directly from the heart to the people. He was as great and real and no bullshit and smart as you would think from his legendary status. And we had FUN. And he went from almost losing everything to winning three Grammys in eight years!

TC: Speaking of legendary performers, how did you meet pianist Henry Butler, and what was your working relationship with him like?

SB: Another long and beautiful story. In the summer of 1984, I was working with the Flying Karamazov Brothers. We spent two months doing a show at the Goodman Theater in Chicago, and then went on to do a second show at the Olympic Arts Festival in LA. When that was over, they invited me up to the Eugene Country Fair, a legendary hippie festival that was associated with Ken Kesey and the Grateful Dead family. When they asked if I’d like to join them on the Old Time New Age Chataqua tour, a traveling group of “New Vaudevillians” – musicians and environmental activists that toured small communities in the rural Northwest, camping out and putting on shows – that seemed like a better option than returning to my non-air-conditioned fifth story walk up apartment on 109th street in July.

Our first stop was our one actual “gig,” at the Vancouver Folk Festival, and we headed up there directly from the Eugene Country Fair, where we had been enjoying the kind of quality research one would associate with the Grateful Dead Community. As we entered the festival, I heard a sound I was not expecting at a folk festival – a piano player, playing and singing music that seemed like it was completely futuristic, and at the same time playing music that seemed to come from early pre-jazz America. I had never heard anything like this, and at first, I thought my ears and brain were still vibrating from my Country Fair adventures, but it was actually being played, and it was (a pre-Impulse records) Henry Butler. He completely changed my DNA and I became a fan, buying his records when they came out.

When the Kansas City soundtrack record came out on Verve records, it was a time of flowing money in the record business, CDs were selling, and I believe the Bertleman Family had bought the Verve company. In 1995 they organized a cross-country tour with the Joe Henderson Trio, Charlie Haden Quartet West, and the Kansas City All-Stars, which included many Verve artists. I was the musical director of a band that included David “Fathead” Newman, Don Byron, Nicholas Payton, Christian McBride, James Carter, Mark Whitfield, etc.

I had contracted the band but was unable to find a piano player (Gerri Allen and Cyrus Chesnut had done the movie). I contacted seemingly every pianist in NYC who would fit the bill, and none were available, and I was starting to panic. I called Hal Willner to ask his advice and without missing a beat he said “did you call Henry Butler?” And that’s how it all started.

Henry and I were kindred spirits and when the tour was over he told me we would work together again. In 2011 I was doing an “MTO Plays the Early Blues” concert at a summer series in NYC. The promoter, Jay Weisman, asked if I’d like to have Henry Butler play, and I said of course, but where is he? It turned out he had an apartment in Brooklyn, post Katrina. When the concert was over Henry called me and said we should do a show with MTO playing all of his music – that was the birth of Butler Bernstein and the Hot 9 (there were 10 people in the band). As far as my working relationship, he totally trusted my bandleading instincts and arranging, and I was always awed and inspired by the music flowing out of him.

TC: You bring up a salient point. Around the time of the Kansas City soundtrack, there seemed to be a very healthy major label interest in jazz that benefitted musicians of all stripes, even those somewhat on the fringe (James Carter, Don Byron, David Murray, etc.), which to me, evoked the pre-Young Lions era, when major labels signed post-loft jazz artists like Anthony Braxton, Arthur Blythe, and Henry Threadgill.

Much has changed since then. I’m curious what your thoughts are on that phenomenon? How have you adapted to the changing fortunes of the recording business? And what do you foresee for the future?

SB: Well, the beautiful thing is that I have been DIY since the beginning. I think the budget of the first Spanish Fly record (which was on Knitting Factory Records) was 3K, and Hal Willner produced it! I personally have never really had a record contract where I was signed and had a budget. I’ve had a few independent contracts, and records funded by public and private grants. That is the way everything is now, so it’s just the way I’ve always been able to create new things. And that’s what it’s about, creating new things.

TC: In reference to creating new things, I’m curious about your thoughts on live performance versus studio recording. Studio recordings of Sexmob often feature a fair amount of electronic manipulation and remixing, much like Ultra Resonance. What are your thoughts on the difference between purely acoustic performances versus such heavily processed and studio manipulated recordings? Do you vary your approach towards playing depending on the situation?

SB: My feeling is that once Electric Ladyland and The White Album came out, there was no turning back. Even my albums that aren’t “heavily electronically processed” (aka produced by Scotty Hard) feature mixes that are very specific, often times emphasizing certain frequencies, the same way a painter will use certain colors to draw the eye. I believe a record should be a mind-altering listening experience. ResoNation Trio is also a studio record, although one that creates a vision of an imagined acoustic experience. As far as playing, I just do the best I can when the recording light is on!

TC: Let’s go back to those early, heady days. According to your bio, you grew up in the Berkeley area and were friends with Peter Apfelbaum, with whom you regularly attended jazz gigs. There was mention of an “eye-opening gig” by the Art Ensemble of Chicago at San Francisco’s Great American Music Hall. What was it about that particular show that resonated with you?

SB: It was just seeing them live after listening to the records for two years. The magic and visceral-ness of it. There is magic that happens when you are in the room, seeing the musicians and feeling the vibrations, sharing the communion of music. We also met them that night. We were pretty heady. We went to their dressing room and banged out “Nfamoudou-Boudougou” on the door. They were certainly shocked to open the door and see two scruffy teenagers.

They welcomed Peter and me into the dressing room, and that started a relationship that continues to this day (Peter is still in touch with Roscoe). When I moved to NYC I went to see the AEC at the Public Theatre, either late 1979 or early 1980. Now when we went to shows in the Bay Area everyone was dressed hippie funky, so that’s how I showed up, probably in overalls and a t-shirt. I go backstage after the show and am totally self-conscious to be surrounded by well-dressed urban New Yorkers in Kente Cloth and immaculate jewelry. Lester opens up the dressing room door, peeks out at all the “beautiful people” and says “BERNSTEIN get in here!” closes the door, points to the table and says “you can roll a joint, right?” (I could).

TC: Now that’s funny. I certainly remember my one and only time seeing the Art Ensemble of Chicago. It was in Philadelphia, at The Clef Club. Jarman wasn’t touring with them at this point, but it was still magical, ceremonial even.

One group I regretfully never saw was The Lounge Lizards. You were a member of The Lounge Lizards in the 1990s. How did that association come about? And while bandleader John Lurie has had an unusual (to say the least) life and career path since then, I was wondering, do you still have any contact with him?

SB: I have yet another tall tale to tell. It was summer of 1989 and I was touring with Chautauqua again, the same group of people I was touring with when I first heard Henry Butler in 1984. Back then we had answering machines that you called into and used a beeper to retrieve your messages (This is pre cell phones). I was in a small town somewhere, probably Idaho or Montana, and I went to a payphone and checked my messages, and I heard a message from John’s assistant saying to call John up because he was interested in having me join The Lounge Lizards. Needless to say I was beyond excited, because The Lounge Lizards was the “Premiere Band” on the downtown scene.

I call John up and the first thing he says to me is “Do you have a suit?” The next thing he says to me is “you’re not gonna get a lot of solos.” Luckily, the tour was heading to a place of general civilization (Port Townsend) and I was able to put together a tape so John had an idea of what my playing was like, and that September I started rehearsing with the band.

I still talk with John. The most recent project we did together was working on music for his film, that was two summers ago. We did music for Painting with John, and there was an excellent and entertaining episode in season three (I believe) that featured the making of the soundtrack, which really showed the process that we use.

Early on with The Lounge Lizards I started to arrange and transcribe for John, first working on Fishing with John, which led to arranging and conducting soundtracks such as Get Shorty and Excess Baggage. Get Shorty was the summer of 1995, and John and I would spend 12 hours a day together as I transcribed his ideas and put them into notated forms.

TC: I’m glad to hear you’re still in contact with John. Speaking of the 1990s, you recorded four albums in the late 1990s to early 2000s for John Zorn’s Radical Jewish Culture series on his Tzadik label: Diaspora Soul (1999); Diaspora Blues (2002); Diaspora Hollywood (2004); and Diaspora Suite (2008). As a fan of those albums, I’m curious if you ever return to any of those tunes or arrangements?

SB: I’m glad you brought up those records. I love the Diaspora series too. Yes, it lives on. I wrote big band arrangements of some of this music for Arturo O’Farril and the Afro Latin Jazz Orchestra for two different concerts. I arranged a version of “Ani Mamin,” which I recorded with saxophones and valve trumpet on Diaspora Soul, reimagined as a tribute to Eddie Palmer and Conjunto Libre, arranged now for four trombones and slide trumpet. I learned that Barry Rogers, the architect of the New York salsa trombone sound, was raised in Brooklyn and his father and uncle sang with Moshe Kousevvitskey’s choir. Full circle New York history for you. I also recorded a version of “Cha” with Arturo and the Afro Latin Jazz Orchestra. We recorded it during the pandemic, so it's all over-dubbed. “Cha” was inspired by John Zorn’s composing for Masada, and I created an arrangement inspired by Machito. I recently revisited the Diaspora Blues music alongside Arturo O’Farrill, Anat Cohen, and a small version of the Afro Latin Jazz Ensemble. This October at the Stone I'll be premiering a duo version of the Diaspora music with Arturo O’Farrill, so the music lives on, and keeps evolving.

TC: What other musical projects or performances do you have coming up in the near future?

SB: Here are a few upcoming shows:

September 23-29: Laurie Anderson and Sexmob, West Coast Tour and Chicago October 1: Helm Family Ramble in Brooklyn October 2: ResoNation Trio at Tempo, Kingston NY October 28: ResoNation Trio at The Stone October 29: Ultra Resonance at The Stone October 30: Diaspora Special Edition with Arturo O’Farrill at The Stone October 31: Sexmob Kurt Weill Halloween at The Stone

Sexmob Live at Carambolage, Bolzano (the last night of our March 2026 European tour) will be released at the end of the year. It’s our first documentation of the “new sound” of the band with Kenny’s electro drums in the mix.

And more upcoming projects that I’m not quite ready to announce.
